title: Thermal Processes
seo_title: Secondary 3 Physics: Thermal Processes Worksheets (O-Level 6091 with Answers)
standard_text: Show understanding that thermal energy is transferred from a region of higher temperature to a region of lower temperature and that regions of equal temperature are in thermal equilibrium; describe, in molecular terms, how energy is transferred by conduction in solids (including by free electrons in metals) and by convection in fluids; describe radiation as transfer by infrared waves that needs no medium; describe the effect of surface colour and texture, surface temperature and surface area on the rate of emission and absorption of radiation; explain everyday applications such as the vacuum flask (summary of the Singapore-Cambridge O-Level Physics 6091 syllabus).
meta_desc: Free Secondary 3 O-Level Physics worksheets on thermal processes: thermal equilibrium, conduction, convection, radiation, good and bad emitters and absorbers, and the vacuum flask. 100 questions with answers.
key_big: Thermal energy flows from hot to cold.
body_html:
How to think about it

Thermal energy always flows from a hotter region to a colder one until they reach thermal equilibrium.

  • Conduction: vibrating particles pass energy on; in metals, free electrons carry energy quickly. Air is a poor conductor.
  • Convection: a heated fluid expands, becomes less dense and rises; cooler, denser fluid sinks, making a convection current.
  • Radiation: infrared waves, no medium needed. Dull black surfaces are good absorbers and emitters; shiny surfaces are poor ones. Hotter and larger surfaces emit faster.
Example

Where should a heater be placed in a room?

warm air rises

cool air sinks to replace it

Answer: near the floor

Example

Which loses heat fastest by radiation: a shiny or a dull black kettle?

dull black is a better emitter

Answer: the dull black kettle

Common mistakes

  • Saying 'cold flows in'. Thermal energy flows out from the hotter object.
  • Saying heat rises. The hot fluid rises because it is less dense.
  • Thinking radiation needs air. It travels through a vacuum.
  • Calling shiny surfaces good emitters. They are poor emitters and good reflectors.

faq.q: What are the three ways thermal energy is transferred?
faq.a: Conduction (through solids by particle collisions and free electrons), convection (by the movement of a heated fluid) and radiation (by infrared waves).

faq.q: Which surfaces are the best emitters and absorbers of radiation?
faq.a: Dull, black surfaces. Shiny, silvery or white surfaces are the poorest emitters and absorbers.

faq.q: How does a vacuum flask keep drinks hot?
faq.a: The vacuum stops conduction and convection, the silvered walls reduce radiation, and the stopper reduces convection and evaporation.

items.q: Why is the heating element of an electric kettle at the bottom?
c: Heated water rises and cooler water sinks, so convection currents heat all the water.
items.e: Convection current.

items.q: Which choice is best for a solar water heater on a roof?
c: Aluminium with fins, because it conducts heat away and has a large surface area.
Polystyrene foam, because it traps air, a poor conductor.
Pipes painted dull black, because they absorb radiation well.
Aluminium, because it is a good conductor of heat.
items.e: Choose good conductors to transfer heat and insulators to stop it.

items.q: Which of these is the worst conductor of heat: glass, aluminium, water, copper?

items.q: When are two objects in thermal equilibrium?
c: when they have the same mass
when they are made of the same material
when there is no net flow of thermal energy between them because they are at the same temperature
items.e: Thermal energy flows from hotter to colder until temperatures are equal.

items.q: Why are liquids and gases poor conductors?
c: They have too many free electrons.
Their particles are further apart, so energy is passed on less easily by collisions.
items.e: Gases are the poorest conductors.

items.q: A sea breeze blows from the sea towards the land in the afternoon. Which process mainly transfers the heat?
items.e: Warmer fluid is less dense and rises; cooler fluid sinks.

items.q: Why are many HDB roofs and walls painted in light colours?

items.q: Why are metals good conductors of heat?

items.e: Free electrons add to particle vibrations.

items.q: Why are solar water heater panels painted dull black?

items.q: Which can of hot water cools fastest: dull black, dull white, shiny silver or shiny white?

items.q: Why can convection not happen in a solid?

items.e: Convection needs a fluid that can flow.

sets.title: Uses: the vacuum flask and everyday examples

items.q: Which choice is best for the walls of a vacuum flask?
c: Polystyrene foam, because it traps air, a poor conductor.
Aluminium, because it is a good conductor of heat.
Plastic, because it is a poor conductor of heat.
Silvered glass, because shiny surfaces reflect radiation.
items.e: Choose good conductors to transfer heat and insulators to stop it.

items.q: A hot drink in a cup with a lid cools more slowly. Which process does the lid mainly reduce?
c: convection and evaporation from the surface
items.e: Hot air and vapour cannot rise away.

items.q: On a sunny day, why does a sea breeze blow from the sea to the land?
c: Water evaporates and pushes the air.
The wind always blows from the sea.
The land heats up faster; air above it rises and cooler air from over the sea moves in to replace it.
items.e: Land has a lower specific heat capacity than water.

items.q: Which part of a vacuum flask are poor conductors, so they reduce conduction?
c: the silvered inner surfaces of the glass walls
the plastic or felt supports holding the inner bottle
the vacuum between the two glass walls
items.e: The plastic or felt supports holding the inner bottle: are poor conductors, so they reduce conduction.

items.q: Which choice is best for a cooler box to keep drinks cold?
c: Aluminium with fins, because it conducts heat away and has a large surface area.
Polystyrene foam, because it traps air, a poor conductor.
Plastic, because it is a poor conductor of heat.
Aluminium, because it is a good conductor of heat.
items.e: Choose good conductors to transfer heat and insulators to stop it.

items.q: Why are cooking pots made of metal with plastic handles?
c: Metal conducts heat to the food quickly; plastic is a poor conductor, so the handle stays cool.
items.e: Choose conductors and insulators for the job.

items.q: At night, why does a land breeze blow from the land to the sea?
c: The land cools faster, so warmer air over the sea rises and cool air from the land moves out to replace it.
The land heats up at night.
items.e: Convection currents reverse at night.

items.q: Which part of a vacuum flask stops conduction and convection?
c: the silvered inner surfaces of the glass walls
the plastic or felt supports holding the inner bottle
the vacuum between the two glass walls
items.e: The vacuum between the two glass walls: stops conduction and convection.

items.q: Which part of a vacuum flask reduces conduction and stops convection and evaporation at the top?
c: the plastic or felt supports holding the inner bottle
the silvered inner surfaces of the glass walls
the vacuum between the two glass walls
items.e: The stopper (cork or plastic): reduces conduction and stops convection and evaporation at the top.

items.q: In a vacuum flask, what does the vacuum between the two glass walls do?
c: reduces conduction and stops convection and evaporation at the top
are poor conductors, so they reduce conduction
items.e: The vacuum between the two glass walls: stops conduction and convection.

items.q: Why are the cooling fins on the back of a fridge painted black?
c: Black is a good emitter of radiation.
items.e: Fins also have a large area.

items.q: Two black metal plates at the same temperature have areas of 0.1 m² and 0.4 m². Which emits more radiation each second?
items.e: A larger surface area emits more radiation.

items.q: In a vacuum flask, what does the silvered inner surfaces of the glass walls do?
c: reduces conduction and stops convection and evaporation at the top
are poor conductors, so they reduce conduction
items.e: The silvered inner surfaces of the glass walls: reduce heat transfer by radiation.

items.q: In a vacuum flask, what does the plastic or felt supports holding the inner bottle do?

are poor conductors, so they reduce conduction
items.e: The plastic or felt supports holding the inner bottle: are poor conductors, so they reduce conduction.

items.q: Why does a double-glazed window reduce heat transfer?
c: The gap allows convection to cool the room.

items.e: A narrow gap also limits convection.

items.q: Why are emergency blankets shiny silver?
c: Shiny surfaces are poor emitters, so less thermal energy is lost by radiation.
Silver conducts heat into the body.
Shiny surfaces absorb more heat from the body.
items.e: Also a good reflector of radiation back to the body.

items.q: Why is an air-conditioner installed high up on a wall?
c: It is out of reach of children only.
The cool air is denser and sinks, setting up a convection current that cools the whole room.
Radiation is stronger near the ceiling.
items.e: Heaters are placed low for the same reason.
